evidence_quote: As of July 2023, its feature films have earned over $17 billion at the worldwide box office with an average gross of $589 million per film.
prompt: A large family-entertainment conglomerate has a long co-production and distribution partnership with a computer-animation studio that has made a string of box-office and critical hits. Talks to extend the partnership broke down over economics and it expires soon. The conglomerate's own hand-drawn animation unit has had several recent underperformers, and the studio could now partner with a rival. Proposal (2006): buy the studio outright for about $7.4 billion in an all-stock deal and put the studio's creative leaders in charge of the conglomerate's animation. Risks raised: the price is very high against a studio that makes about one film a year; culture clash; dependence on a few creative leaders; the studio's largest shareholder (a famous founder) would become a major shareholder of the buyer.

evidence_quote: The franchise has been commercially successful, becoming one of the highest-grossing media franchises of all time
prompt: A family-entertainment conglomerate with strong girl- and young-child franchises but weak reach with boys proposes (2009) to buy a comics publisher and character licensor for about $4 billion, paid in cash plus stock. The target has just started producing its own films after years of licensing characters to other studios; its first self-financed film did well, but its slate of films is short and unproven, and its most famous characters were already licensed to rivals under long-term deals. Risks raised: price, creative-control disputes with the target's leaders, licensing encumbrances, and the cyclical nature of comics-based films.

evidence_quote: reaching 1 million registered users in two months, 10 million in a year, and 1 billion in June 2018
prompt: A dominant social network is about to go public. It proposes (April 2012) to buy a photo-sharing mobile app with about a dozen employees and no revenue, for about $1 billion in cash and stock. The app has tens of millions of users, is growing fast on one phone platform and has just launched on the other, and is seen as the leading mobile threat to the buyer's own photo product. Risks raised: valuation far above any revenue, no business model, the buyer's own weak mobile product, regulatory review, and the risk of destroying the app's culture.

evidence_quote: In January 2024, YouTube had reached more than 2.7 billion monthly active users
prompt: A search company proposes (October 2006) to buy a 20-month-old video-sharing site for $1.65 billion in stock. The site is the largest online video destination, with a very small staff, high bandwidth bills, no meaningful revenue, and a large volume of user uploads of copyrighted TV and film clips. Media companies have threatened lawsuits. The buyer already runs its own video service, which is smaller. Risks raised: price, copyright litigation exposure, unproven ad model for video, and bandwidth cost at scale.

evidence_quote: In April 2015, Amazon.com reported AWS was profitable, with sales of $1.57 billion in the first quarter of the year and $265 million of operating income.
prompt: An online retailer with thin margins and a large, spiky internal infrastructure build-out proposes (2006) to sell rented computing and storage (pay-per-use servers and object storage) to outside developers and companies, as a new business line distinct from retail. No one in the company has run a developer platform business at scale; large incumbent hardware and software vendors exist; investors already question the retailer's heavy capital spending; and the market for renting servers by the hour is unproven. Risks raised: distraction from the core business, margin dilution, reliability expectations, and competition from established vendors.

evidence_quote: its stores were highly successful, bypassing the sales numbers of competing nearby stores and within three years reached US$1 billion in annual sales
prompt: A personal-computer maker with about 3 to 5 percent market share, a recent run of losses, and sales through third-party electronics retailers (where staff push cheaper competing machines) proposes (2001) to open its own chain of company-run retail stores in prime shopping-mall locations. Computer retail has low margins and the stores would carry high lease costs. Management argues stores are needed to demonstrate the product and its new digital-music strategy. Risks raised: fixed lease costs during a recession, inventory risk, channel conflict with resellers, and a poor retail track record in the industry.

evidence_quote: with over 155 million units shipped worldwide as of December 2025, it is the second-best-selling console
prompt: A console maker's previous home console sold poorly and caused financial losses; its handheld line is being eroded by phones. Proposal (late 2016): release a new hybrid machine that works both docked to a TV and as a handheld, using a modest-power mobile chip, with detachable motion controllers, priced about the same as rival consoles that are far more powerful, launching with a thin first-year game line-up from the maker's own studios. Risks raised: weak hardware specs against rivals, confusing positioning after the last console's confusing launch, limited third-party support, supply constraints, and short window to recover.

evidence_quote: it was the first mass-produced hybrid vehicle, first going on sale in Japan in 1997
prompt: A large automaker proposes (mid-1990s) to commit to mass-producing a petrol-electric hybrid passenger car by 1997, as a corporate-level programme with a bold public schedule, using a novel power-split transmission and nickel-metal-hydride battery pack, a first for volume production. Fuel is cheap in the main export market, regulators have not mandated hybrids, no competitor has a production hybrid, and battery durability is unproven. Risks raised: cost, reliability and warranty exposure, and no near-term demand signal.

evidence_quote: As of January 2023, GitHub reported having over 100 million developers and more than 420 million repositories
prompt: A large software company that was historically hostile to open source and has since pivoted to embrace it proposes (June 2018) to buy the dominant code-hosting service for about $7.5 billion in stock. The target is loss-making, has been without a permanent chief executive for months, and has a developer community that is vocal about distrust of the buyer; alternatives like a free competitor are being touted by users. The target would run independently under the buyer. Risks raised: developer defection, price versus revenue, regulatory scrutiny, and antitrust sensitivity.

evidence_quote: a year after the launch of Disney+, it had over 86.8 million subscribers
prompt: A major film and TV conglomerate earns billions from licensing its library and theatrical releases to other streaming services and cable. Proposal (2019): pull its content from rivals, launch its own subscription streaming service at a low price (below the market leader's), and fund it with a multi-year operating loss while it builds an audience. Management targets tens of millions of subscribers within five years; the leading service already has well over a hundred million subscribers. Risks raised: loss of licensing revenue, the cash burn, execution of a technology platform the company has never run, and cannibalisation of cable and theatrical revenue.

evidence_quote: this was Google's "best deal ever" according to Google's then-vice president of corporate development
prompt: A search-advertising company with no hardware business proposes (July 2005) to acquire a tiny, secretive startup of about six people that is building an open-source mobile phone operating system, for at least $50 million. The phone market is dominated by established OS vendors and a few handset makers that have no reason to adopt a new platform; carriers control distribution. The bet is that free, open software will push mobile web use and thus search ad revenue. Risks raised: no revenue model, handset-maker adoption, carrier resistance, and a long multi-year payback.

evidence_quote: CUDA became central to the company's strategy of positioning GPUs as versatile hardware for scientific applications.
prompt: A graphics-chip maker whose revenue comes almost entirely from gaming and workstation graphics proposes (2004 to 2006) a multi-year programme to make its mass-market graphics chips programmable for general scientific computing: add chip area for general-purpose features, build a full compiler and software toolchain, and fund university teaching, all on every consumer chip it sells, raising unit cost. No large paying market for GPU computing exists yet; academic users are experimenting with hacked graphics APIs. Risks raised: cost on every unit, no committed customers, engineering distraction from its core race with its main rival, and niche demand.

evidence_quote: Apple has sold an estimated 450 million iPods.
prompt: A computer maker with a small market share and no consumer-electronics experience proposes (early 2001) to build a pocket digital-music player with a 5 GB hard drive in under a year, priced at roughly $400, sold only with its own computers' music software (so initially only owners of its own small-share computers could use it). Several cheaper digital music players exist and have not sold well; the music industry has not yet licensed legal downloads at scale; the player would priced above typical competitors. Risks raised: price, tiny addressable base of compatible computers, and component sourcing in a short timeline.

evidence_quote: claims to have paid over $320 billion to developers
prompt: A phone maker whose first-generation smartphone launched a year earlier, and whose chief executive had publicly argued that web apps were sufficient, proposes (2008) to open the phone to third-party native apps via a single company-run store: developers set prices, the company keeps 30 percent, and the company reviews and approves every app. Concerns: security and stability risk from untrusted code, carrier objections to apps that bypass their services, review workload, and the possibility that apps hurt the polish of the product. Rival platforms already have app ecosystems with open distribution.

evidence_quote: House of Cards received highly positive reviews and numerous award nominations, including 33 Primetime Emmy Award nominations
prompt: A subscription video service that has mainly licensed other companies' content, and whose licensing costs are rising, proposes (early 2011) to commission its first big-budget original drama: a straight-to-series order of two full seasons (26 episodes) with a well-known film director and a film star attached, with no pilot, released all at once instead of weekly. Broadcasters normally test a pilot first; no online-only service has produced a prestige scripted series; the cost is a large share of its content budget. The case for it relies on the service's viewing data. Risks raised: no pilot de-risking, uncertain audience, and cost.

evidence_quote: Netflix is the most-subscribed video on demand global streaming media service, with 325 million paid memberships
prompt: A profitable mail-order DVD rental company with about seven million subscribers proposes (2007) to add an online streaming option at no extra charge for existing subscribers, even though the streaming catalogue is small and mostly older titles, video quality is poor, broadband is not universal, studios license streaming rights at high prices, and big technology and retail companies are expected to enter. Streaming could cannibalise the profitable DVD business. Risks raised: content licensing cost, cannibalisation, technology cost, and the strategic risk of competing with far larger entrants.

evidence_quote: Total lifetime sales of the Wii reached over 101 million units.
prompt: A console maker in third place in the console market proposes (2005 to 2006) to skip the graphics-power race and instead sell a low-cost console with modest hardware (not high-definition) built around a motion-sensing controller aimed at casual and non-gamers, pricing it far below rival high-definition consoles and launching with simple, family-friendly games. Hardcore gamers and third-party publishers are sceptical; the controller is unusual; the hardware margin is thin. Risks raised: limited third-party support, perception as a toy, no high-definition output, and an untested casual audience.

evidence_quote: As of May 2025, the service had 3 billion monthly active users, making it the most popular messenger app.
prompt: A social network with a large user base proposes (February 2014) to buy a fast-growing cross-platform messaging app for $19 billion in cash and stock; the target was valued at $1.5 billion in a financing round a year earlier, has about 50 employees, charges a $1 yearly fee and has minimal revenue, and has refused to show advertising. The target has hundreds of millions of monthly users, the buyer fears mobile messaging apps are displacing its own services. It would be the buyer's largest acquisition ever and the largest purchase of a venture-backed company. Risks raised: price (many times the prior valuation), no monetisation plan, privacy regulation, and founder-retention.

evidence_quote: Its 2001 merger with AOL, which formed AOL Time Warner, became one of worst business deals in corporate history, which led the company to revert its name to Time Warner in 2003.
prompt: An internet-access provider with about 20 million dial-up subscribers and a very high stock valuation proposes (January 2000) an all-stock merger with the world's largest traditional media conglomerate (film, magazines, cable TV and music), forming a combined company in which the internet provider's shareholders hold a majority. Pitch: combine content with distribution, cross-promote magazines, films and music over the internet, and deliver high-speed access over the conglomerate's cable network. The conglomerate's board sees a premium to its stock. Concerns: the internet company's valuation is volatile and its dial-up business may decline as broadband spreads; cable partners' network access isn't guaranteed; cultures differ; regulators must approve.

evidence_quote: It launched in April 2020, but shut down in December 2020 after falling short of its subscriber projections.
prompt: A veteran film-industry executive proposes (2018) to raise well over $1 billion to launch a new mobile-only subscription video service of short-form, professionally produced shows (episodes under 10 minutes), with high production budgets, A-list talent, and a technology feature that makes video look right whether the phone is held vertically or horizontally. Free ad-supported short video (including user-generated content) is abundant on existing platforms; subscription fatigue is a rising concern. Investors include several major studios and brands. Risks raised: no proven demand for premium short-form, price, and competition for phone attention.

evidence_quote: In 2015, Microsoft took a US$7.8 billion (~$10.1 billion in 2024) write-down on the Nokia purchase
prompt: A software company whose mobile operating system holds a low single-digit share of smartphones proposes (2013) to buy the handset division of the main manufacturer of devices running that system, for about €5.4 billion, to control hardware and software together and stop the manufacturer from switching to the market-leading rival platform. The handset maker's smartphone sales are falling and the market leader's platform has most of the apps and developers. Risks raised: integration of a large workforce, other handset makers' reaction, and whether hardware ownership can fix an app-ecosystem problem.

evidence_quote: Within a year, HP had written off $8.8 billion of Autonomy's value.
prompt: A large hardware company with a new chief executive wants to move toward software and enterprise data analytics. It proposes (August 2011) to buy a UK enterprise-search and analytics software company for about $11.7 billion, roughly 64 percent above the target's recent share price and about 11 times its revenue. The hardware company's own finance chief is reported to have reservations about the price; the target's financial reporting has been questioned in the press since 2009. Due diligence is being done in a few weeks. Risks raised: price, accounting quality, integration, and the buyer's lack of software experience.

evidence_quote: the move effectively puts the final nail in the coffin of a product that was launched in 2011 to challenge Facebook, and is widely seen as one of Google's biggest failures
prompt: A search company, whose three previous social-networking attempts did not take off, proposes (2011) a company-wide push to launch its own social network to challenge the market leader (which already has hundreds of millions of users), by integrating a new profile and sharing layer into its search, mail, video, and photo products, with executive bonuses tied to its adoption, and launching with an invite-only beta. Differentiators are friend-grouping circles and video hangouts. Risks raised: network effects favour the incumbent, users may not switch, forced integration may annoy existing users, and the company has a history of failed social products.

evidence_quote: based in part on its quickly declining prices and an announced US$170 million write-down, analysts have judged it a commercial failure
prompt: An online retailer that has had success with an e-reader and a low-priced tablet proposes (June 2014) to launch its own smartphone, sold exclusively through one US carrier at an unsubsidised-equivalent price in line with leading flagship phones, with a headline feature of a 3D-like display driven by front-facing cameras and head tracking, and a one-touch way to identify products for purchase. The phone uses a forked mobile OS with a smaller app store, without the leading platform's own mainstream apps. The smartphone market is dominated by two platforms. Risks raised: price versus differentiation, app gap, carrier exclusivity, and a market already saturated.

evidence_quote: Quaker Oats ran into problems and sold Snapple to Triarc in 1997 for $300 million.
prompt: A food and beverage company that owns a leading sports drink proposes (1994) to acquire a fast-growing premium ready-to-drink tea and juice brand for about $1.7 billion in cash. The brand has a small, quirky network of independent distributors, strong growth, and strong consumer loyalty. The buyer plans to move the brand into its own supermarket-focused distribution and mass-market advertising, as it did with its sports drink. Risks raised: the independent distributors' loyalty, whether the brand's cult image survives corporate marketing, price, and increasing competition from large soft-drink companies' tea launches.

evidence_quote: Daimler agreed to sell the Chrysler unit to Cerberus Capital Management in May 2007 for US$6 billion
prompt: A premium German carmaker proposes (1998) a stock-for-stock merger of equals with the third-largest US automaker, which is highly profitable at the moment on trucks, minivans and SUVs, to form a global automaker with a combined board and a new combined stock listing. The pitch is global scale, complementary brands and platform sharing, and entry into the North American mass market. Concerns: very different corporate and labour cultures, the US partner's dependence on a cyclical light-truck boom, the German firm's premium-brand positioning, and whether it is truly a merger of equals or a takeover.

evidence_quote: Within three months, the Coca-Cola Company reintroduced the original formula under the name "Coca-Cola Classic"
prompt: The market leader in cola, which has been losing share to diet soft drinks and non-cola beverages for several years, finds in blind taste tests that consumers prefer its main rival's sweeter drink; a sweeter new formula beats both the old formula and the rival in taste tests, surveys and focus groups. It proposes (1985) to replace its century-old flagship formula with the new sweeter one, and withdraw the original from sale entirely. Testing did not tell participants the original would be removed. Risks raised: emotional attachment to the original, brand heritage, no fallback product, and reaction among loyal bottlers and consumers.

evidence_quote: In 2017, following slow sales, Juicero ceased operations and announced it was seeking a complete buyout.
prompt: A well-funded consumer-hardware startup that has raised tens of millions of dollars proposes (early 2016) to launch a Wi-Fi-connected countertop juicer priced at $699 that presses proprietary pre-packed bags of chopped fruit and vegetables bought by subscription, with a custom-engineered press and an app tied to the device that checks pack freshness. Concerns: the high device price, the subscription price per bag versus buying produce and juicing it, the requirement for internet connectivity, and the size of the market.

evidence_quote: In December 2018, Verizon announced it would write-down the combined value of its purchases of AOL and Yahoo by $4.6 billion, roughly half
prompt: A large wireless carrier that bought a legacy internet media and advertising company the previous year proposes (July 2016) to buy the core operating business of another declining internet portal for about $4.8 billion. The aim is to combine the two to build a mobile media and advertising business scaled enough to compete with the two dominant online ad platforms. The target's traffic and ad revenue have been falling for years, it has had repeated management changes, and the carrier has no history in consumer media. Risks raised: ad-revenue decline, and integration.

evidence_quote: Netflix's stock value dropped, and 800,000 of its 12 million customers cancelled their subscriptions. Netflix quickly apologized, and in October 2011, announced it would retain its DVD service under the name Netflix
prompt: A subscription service that offers both DVD-by-mail and online streaming in a single combined plan has just raised the combined price by about 60 percent for customers who want both (July 2011). Proposal (September 2011): split the DVD-by-mail business into a separate brand and website, with a new name, its own account and queue, and separate billing; streaming keeps the existing brand. The two services' ratings and recommendations would not be shared. Rationale: the DVD business is declining and needs different management, and streaming should be free to pursue its own strategy. Risks raised: customer confusion and having two logins and bills, loss of cross-service recommendations, and reaction to the price increase.

evidence_quote: The retail chain racked up losses of $2.1 billion in its lifespan, and was widely viewed as a failure
prompt: A large US discount retailer with a loyal domestic following proposes (2011) its first international expansion: buying leases for around 130 to 150 existing store sites in a neighbouring country and opening nearly all of them within about two years, supplied by a new supply chain and a new inventory-management system. The local market is dominated by a larger, entrenched competitor and has higher prices on some goods; the retailer would have to learn cross-border logistics, regulation and bilingual labelling. Risks raised: the pace of opening many stores at once, new supply chain systems not yet proven, and price perception.

evidence_quote: Johnson was dismissed in April 2013 and replaced by former CEO Mike Ullman.
prompt: A mid-market US department store chain with falling sales and an older, coupon-driven customer base appoints (2011) as chief executive the executive who built a hugely successful chain of branded electronics stores, who proposes (January 2012) to end the constant sales-and-coupons model in favour of simple everyday pricing with fewer promotions, and to rebuild stores into a set of branded in-store shops. Most of the chain's sales have historically come from items sold at a discount. The plan is announced without a test in a few stores. Risks raised: existing customers trained to wait for coupons, no pilot, and the pace of changing the entire chain at once.

evidence_quote: Webvan was a dot-com company and grocery business that filed for bankruptcy in 2001 after three years of operation.
prompt: An online grocery-delivery startup that has just begun taking orders in its first metropolitan area (June 1999) and has raised large amounts of venture capital proposes to place an order of about $1 billion for the construction of highly automated, very large regional warehouses in over a dozen metropolitan areas, plus a fleet of delivery trucks, and to enter new cities at a rapid pace before learning the unit economics of the first. Groceries are a low-margin business. Customers pick a 30-minute delivery slot. Risks raised: capital intensity, thin margins, customer-density needs, and no operating track record.

evidence_quote: On July 2, 2012, Microsoft announced that it would take a $6.2 billion writedown, mostly related to the 2007 acquisition of aQuantive.
prompt: A software company whose search advertising is far behind the market leader proposes (May 2007) to buy a digital advertising agency and ad-serving platform for about $6 billion in cash, its largest acquisition ever, at a large premium. The aim is to own the technology that serves display ads and compete with the search leader, which just agreed to buy another ad-serving platform. Concerns: price, conflicts with the buyer's existing agency customers, and the fast-changing display-ad technology market.

evidence_quote: wrote down $29.7 billion of the $36 billion sum it had paid for Nextel in 2005
prompt: A national wireless carrier proposes (2005) to merge with the smaller carrier whose push-to-talk walkie-talkie service is popular with construction and business customers. The deal, valued at about $36 billion, combines two networks that use different, incompatible technologies. The target has a high-value business customer base, but its network technology is incompatible with the buyer's and limited for data; the combined company must integrate two networks and run one on legacy equipment. Risks raised: technology incompatibility, integration cost, and the large goodwill the buyer would take on.

evidence_quote: a loss of over $250 million (equivalent to $2.72 billion in 2025 dollars) on development, manufacturing, and marketing on the model line
prompt: The second-largest US automaker proposes (mid-1950s) to launch a new mid-priced car division, with its own brand, dealerships and a line of models, to fill a perceived gap between its low-priced and its premium lines and compete with the leader's mid-priced divisions. Extensive market research and consumer-motivation studies shaped the styling and brand, with a massive advertising and teaser campaign planned for a 1957 debut. The mid-priced segment has been growing but could shrink; a recession risk exists; the programme needs a new dealer network. Risks raised: market-segment timing, overlap with the firm's own other brands, and cost of dealer infrastructure.
